list.listitem: Hypoparathyroidism is a rare endocrine disorder. If hypoparathyroidism is suspected (ie, incidental hypocalcemia) measure serum parathyroid hormone (PTH), serum ionized calcium and total calcium-corrected for albumin. C
In patients with hypothyroidism without a history of neck surgery or hemodialysis, exclude hypomagnesemia and vitamin D deficiency as contributing factors. C
Vitamin D analogues and calcium salts increase calcium uptake from the gut and are the primary therapy; they are required for the remainder of the patient's lifetime. C
Recombinant human parathyroid hormone is approved for adjunctive treatment to prevent hypocalcemia. B
Thiazide diuretics decrease excretion of calcium in urine and can be a useful adjunct to vitamin D and calcium therapy, but data is currently very weak. C

background.definition: Hypoparathyroidism is an endocrine disorder characterized by low serum PTH concentration, which can lead to hypocalcemia.

list.listitem: The incidence of hypoparathyroidism is extimated to be 0.8 per 100 000 person-years.
In one study, hypoparathyroidism occurred in 6% of patients following thyroid surgery due to damage or removal of the parathyroid glands.
A study found hypoparathyroidism in 31% to 33% of patients on hemodialysis, and another showed 15% relative hypoparathyroidism following a kidney transplant.
Chromosome 22q11.2 deletion occurs in 1 case per 2000-5000 live births and is the most common human contiguous gene deletion.

Parathyroid gland damage or removal during neck surgery is the most common cause of hypoparathyroidism. Approximately 78 % of cases of hypoparathyroidism are caused by neck surgery, 9% by other secondary causes, 7% by familial disorder and 6% by idiopathic causes. One study of 117,342 surgical cases showed that approximately 38 % of cases occur following total thyroidectomy, 21% of cases after a parathyroidectomy, 9% after partial thyroidectomy and 5% after other neck surgery.
Hemithyroidectomy may be an option for some conditions, and leads to decreased rate of temporary (NNT=5) or permanent (NNT=56) hypoparathyroidism, compared to total thyroidectomy.
Administration of calcium carbonate during hemodialysis can lead to elevated serum calcium, which inhibits PTH secretion. This is thought to contribute to decreased bone remodeling.
Severe hypomagnesemia suppresses secretion of PTH and reduces responsiveness to PTH, leading to hypocalcemia.
Some anticonvulsants deactivate vitamin D and thereby impair PTH's effect on intestinal absorption of calcium.

Congenital defects of the parathyroid glands, leading to deficits in gland function, are seen in chromosome 22q11.2 microdeletion conditions such as DiGeorge syndrome and velocardiofacial syndrome (see History and Physical section). Chromosome 10p terminal deletions are also associated with DiGeorge phenotype and HDR syndrome (hypoparathyroidism, sensorineural deafness and renal dysplasia).

Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy (APECED) is a primary immunodeficiency disorder that includes chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and immune-mediated endocrinopathies, with hypoparathyroidism occurring in 63-96% of cases.
There are rare cases of mutations in the PTH gene, leading either to defective hormone or to an undetectable serum PTH level.
Autosomal dominant hypercalciuric hypocalcemia is caused by mutations of the parathyroid and renal calcium sensing receptors, leading to inappropriate inhibition of PTH secretion by calcium.

Parathyroid hormone is secreted by the 4 parathyroid glands located on the posterior surface to the lobes of the thyroid gland. The secretion of PTH is regulated by a calcium-sensing receptor on the chief cells of the parathyroid gland which is inactivated by hypocalcemia resulting in increased PTH secretion. PTH increases serum calcium by increasing bone resorption and increasing calcium absorption in both the intestines and kidneys. PTH is necessary for renal production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D; therefore, active vitamin D is usually also deficient in hypoparathyroidism.
PTH's promotion of calcium absorption from the gut is decreased in cases of vitamin D deficiency.
Measure serum PTH as well as serum ionized calcium or total calcium-corrected for albumin when hypoparathyroidism is suspected (i.e. incidental hypocalcemia). C
In patients with hypoparathyroidism without a history of neck surgery or hemodialysis, exclude hypomagnesemia and vitamin D deficiency as contributing factors. C

A diagnosis of hypoparathyroidism in a patient who has not had neck surgery, is not receiving hemodialysis, and has normal serum magnesium should spur investigation for other possible endocrine disorders in the patient and his/her relatives. C

Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type I may present in infants and children with a persistent mucous membrane or skin candidal infections. Obtain PTH and ionized calcium levels for patients with this presentation. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Serum vitamin D less than 10 ng/mL; history of anticonvulsant therapy

list.listitem: Clinical features include paresthesia, muscle cramps, muscle spasms, prolong QTC, seizure, laryngospasm, and arrhythmia.
Other manifestations include cataract, enamel hypoplasia of the tooth, increase risk of infection and, cardiovascular disease.

Hypocalcemia may be demonstrated on physical examination by testing for Chvostek's or Trousseau's signs. Chvostek's sign is contractions of the facial muscle subsequent to percussion of the ipsilateral facial nerve anterior to the external auditory meatus. Trousseau's sign is carpal spasm following compression of the arm for 3 minutes with a sphygmomanometer.
Hypoparathyroidism is associated with steatorrhea which may improve with primary treatment or use of medium-chain triglycerides.
DiGeorge syndrome classically consists of hypocalcemia (from hypoplasia of the parathyroid gland), conotruncal cardiac anomalies, and a hypoplastic thymus.

Features of velocardiofacial syndrome can include retrognathia, vertically elongated face, prominent nose, microcephaly, cleft palate, weak pharyngeal musculature, generalized hypotonia, and transient hypocalcemia in approximately 20% of affected neonates.

Initial blood test includes serum ionized calcium or total calcium-corrected for albumin, phosphate and intact PTH. A serum ionized calcium level less than 4.4 mg/dL is abnormal, as is corrected total calcium < 8.4 mg/dL and serum intact PTH value of less than 10 ng/L is abnormal. Also measure serum magnesium (<1.8 mg/dL is abnormal) and serum 25-OH vitamin D (<10 ng/mL is abnormal).
ECG changes can result from hypocalcemia. These include prolongation of the QT interval, as well as QRS and ST-segment changes.

The diagnosis of hypoparathyroidism in a patient who has not had neck surgery, is not receiving hemodialysis, and has a normal serum magnesium should spur investigation for other possible endocrine disorders in the patient and his/her relatives.

Measurement of intraoperative or early postoperative intact PTH following thyroidectomy can help guide patient management. Post-operative PTH < 15 pg/mL increases the risk for hypoparathyroidism and can be treated with empiric or prophylactic oral calcium and vitamin D.
In one series of 54 patients undergoing thyroidectomy, no patient with a normal serum 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D level < 33.5 pg/ml developed hypercalciuria.
Periodic monitoring of calcium, phosphate, creatinine levels, and urinary calcium excretion is required for adequate treatment for hypoparathyroidism.

Suspect hypoparathyroidism in the differential diagnosis of paresthesias, muscle spasms, or seizures, all of which may be manifestations of acute hypocalcemia. Persistent candidal infections of mucous membranes or skin in infants or children may be a presentation of autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type I, which includes hypoparathyroidism.

Measure serum PTH and serum ionized calcium; values of serum PTH less than 10 ng/L, serum ionized calcium less than 4.4 mg/dL, and corrected total calcium <8.4 mg/dL. are diagnostic for hypoparathyroidism.

Initial treatment of tetany and seizure include IV 10% calcium gluconate or 10% calcium chloride infusion (which can only be administered centrally). Acute calcium can lead to arrhythmias, so cardiac monitoring is required. C
Oral vitamin D analogues and calcium salts increase calcium uptake from the gut and are the primary therapy for hypoparathyroidism; these are required for the remainder of the patient's lifetime.
Thiazide diuretics decrease the excretion of calcium in the urine and may be a useful adjunct to vitamin D and calcium therapy, but data suggest that the evidence is very weak. C

The primary therapy for hypoparathyroidism is oral vitamin D analogues (e.g. both cholecalciferol and ergocalciferol can be given at dosage of 400-4000 IU/day with calcitriol or 10,000 -100,000 IU/day without calcitriol) and calcium salts (e.g. calcium carbonate 0.5-2 g divided into 2-4 doses per day with meals) to increase calcium uptake from the gut; these are required for the remainder of the patient's lifetime. An acidic environment is required for absorption of calcium, so calcium citrate would be needed in patients taking acid inhibitors.
Long term calcium target should be at or slightly below lower limit of normal range (approximately 7.8-8.5 mg/dl).

Thiazide diuretics decrease the excretion of calcium in the urine and can be a useful adjunct when serum calcium remains low despite vitamin D and calcium therapy, but evidence is weak. Patient should also be on a low sodium diet.

In patients on dialysis, administration of the noncalcemic phosphate binder sevelamer hydrochloride, in doses of either 6 g/d or 3 g/d depending on serum phosphate levels, reduced calcium concentration and increased serum PTH levels, improving bone remodeling.

Recombinant human PTH 1–84 is approved for the treatment of hypoparathyroidism in the United States in patient who did not respond to conventional therapy except for patients with autosomal dominant hypocalcemia (since those group of patients weren’t included in the clinical trials). It carries a black box warning for an increased risk of osteosarcoma. Recombinant human PTH 1–84 can be given subcutaneously starting at 50 ug/day. Adjust the dose to 25 ug every 4 week with a max dose of 100 ug/day.
Parathyroid autograft is possible but is rarely used due to the subsequent requirement for chronic immunosuppression.
Endocrinology referral upon initial diagnosis is appropriate for all cases of hypoparathyroidism.
Acute hypocalcemia with seizures or tetany requires emergent treatment with IV calcium, as well as management of possible airway and cardiac complications.
Post-surgical hypocalcemia can be a complication of total thyroidectomy. Standard therapy is vitamin D analogues and calcium supplementation.

If IV calcium is the treatment, the initial infusion should consist of 10% calcium gluconate solution, which contains 93 mg of elemental calcium/10 mL over 10 to 15 minutes. Followed by continuous infusion of 1.25 mg of elemental calcium per kg of body weight per hour should be repeated, with close monitoring of serum level, until signs and symptoms of hypocalcemia resolve.
In cases of hypocalcemia along with hypomagnesemia, magnesium replacement (e.g. 100 mEq IV over the first 24 hours) is indicated.
Most patients with DiGeorge syndrome or velocardiofacial syndrome die in early childhood from infections, seizures secondary to hypocalcemia, or cardiac complications. C
Replacement therapy with calcium salts and vitamin D analogues is required lifelong for most patients with hypoparathyroidism. C
A systematic review of 5 studies concluded that treatment of hypoparathyroidism with calcium and vitamin D is associated with a lower quality of life in the long term. B
Long term complications from hypoparathyroidism include seizures, kidney stones, hospitalization for hypocalcemia, and cramps. C

Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type I may present in infants and children with persistent mucous membrane or skin candidal infections. Suspect hypoparathyroidism in patients with this presentation, and obtain serum PTH and ionized calcium levels.

Clinically evaluate infants and children found to have hypocalcemia, conotruncal heart lesions, or cleft palate for DiGeorge syndrome and velocardiofacial syndrome. Characteristics of these syndromes are described in the History and Physical section.

In an RCT of 12 children with chronic hypoparathyroidism, there were no significant differences at 3 year follow-up in height and weight (normal), calcium levels, or bone density between use of twice-daily calcitriol (plus calcium and cholecalciferol in 4 daily doses) versus twice daily subcutaneous PTH 1-34 treatment.
